idiom_name: (a, b) match { case (c: Circle, s: Square) => ... }
implementation_notes: Scala resolves both axes in one construct: matching a tuple with type patterns dispatches on the runtime classes of both operands, and sealed hierarchies make the compiler warn when a case is missing (-Xfatal-warnings turns that into an error). This replaces the visitor for hierarchies you own; note that exhaustiveness is only proven for sealed types, and that the compiler cannot prove disjointness for arbitrary class patterns, so a remaining fallback case is still a runtime path. When the pair set must stay open, a type class (see type-class-dispatch) is Scala's true multiple dispatch.
code_sketch:
sealed trait Shape
final case class Circle(radius: Double) extends Shape
final case class Square(side: Double) extends Shape

def collide(a: Shape, b: Shape): String = (a, b) match {
  case (c: Circle, s: Square) => s"circle ${c.radius} vs square ${s.side}"
  case (s: Square, c: Circle) => collide(c, s)     // canonicalise symmetric pairs
  case (_: Circle, _: Circle) => "two circles"
  case (_: Square, _: Square) => "two squares"
}
pitfalls: Exhaustiveness is a warning by default: a new Shape subtype compiles until -Xfatal-warnings (or a total function) is enabled.
Type patterns are erased for generic types: matching (a: List[Int], b: List[String]) matches on List only and warns unchecked.
Building (a, b) allocates a Tuple2 per call; match on a lightweight key or on the operands separately in hot paths.

variants.name: Type class per pair (open multiple dispatch)
variants.idiom_name: implicit Collision[A, B] instances resolved by implicit search
variants.implementation_notes: Encode the pair as a type class: `trait Collision[A, B]` with one instance per pair, resolved by implicit search, plus a low-priority symmetric derivation for commutative operations. This is Scala's genuine multiple dispatch - new types and new pairs can be added from anywhere without editing existing code or recompiling third-party modules - at the cost of implicit-search complexity, slower compiles and errors that are hard to read. Ambiguity between two equally specific instances is a compile error rather than a silent pick, which is the trade this variant makes for openness. Scala 3 expresses the same idea with given/using.
pitfalls: A symmetric flip instance next to explicit instances creates ambiguity or diverging implicit search unless it is pushed into a low-priority parent trait.
Implicit search silently prefers the most specific instance, so a (Shape, Shape) instance can shadow the pair you expected.
Implicit parameters hide the dispatch from the call site: readers need an IDE to see which instance ran.
